subject: prompt-engineering
question: Does this test show v2 is better?

artifact.prompt:
Prompt v2 adds 'Think step by step'. The author tried 3 questions: v1 got 2 right, v2 got 3 right.
Conclusion: "v2 is 50% better."

ai_claim: Yes. v2 answered 3 of 3 correctly against v1's 2 of 3, which is 50% more correct answers.

failure.misconception: Drawing conclusions from a tiny sample
failure.explanation: A difference of one question out of three is well within random variation; rerunning v1 might give 3/3. Model outputs also vary between runs. Compare prompts on a fixed, representative set (e.g. 200 cases), run several times if sampling is involved, and look at per-case differences.
failure.why_convincing: The arithmetic is correct and the direction looks clear.

canonical_solution: No: one question out of three is noise. Evaluate on a large fixed set.

valid_evidence.summary: Rerunning v1 on the same 3 questions gives 3/3 on the second attempt.
On 200 questions, v1 scores 81% and v2 82%.

counterexamples: A second run of v1 matches v2.

hints.text: Count the evidence behind the conclusion.
Step 4 generalises from 3 questions.
Small samples cannot distinguish real improvements from noise.
Rerun v1.
Step 4 is wrong: 3 questions cannot show a difference.

repair: Build a fixed evaluation set of at least a few hundred representative cases.
debrief: Prompt tweaking without a real evaluation set is guessing with extra steps.

subject: prompt-engineering
subtopic: Tuning until the eval set is perfect
question: Does 60/60 show the prompt extracts perfectly on new documents?

artifact.prompt:
A team revised their extraction prompt 40 times, each time checking accuracy on the same 60-document evaluation set, until it reached 60/60.
Claim: "The prompt now extracts perfectly."

ai_claim: Yes. The prompt gets every evaluation document right, so it extracts perfectly.

ai_solution.text: The final prompt gets all 60 right.
The evaluation set represents real documents.

failure.misconception: Overfitting a prompt to its evaluation set
failure.explanation: After 40 revisions guided by the same 60 documents, the prompt has been tuned to their quirks (special-case instructions for particular layouts). The set no longer gives an unbiased estimate. Keep a separate held-out test set that is not used during iteration, and measure on it only at the end.
failure.why_convincing: Prompts do not have weights, so overfitting seems impossible.

canonical_solution: No: the prompt was tuned on these 60 documents. Measure on a held-out set.

valid_evidence.summary: revisions 31-40 each added a rule for one specific failing document

hints.text: Ask how many decisions were made using this set.
Step 3 assumes the set is still unbiased.
Iterating against one set overfits to it, even for prompts.
Test on new documents.
Step 3 is wrong: the prompt is overfit to the eval set.

repair: Split into a development set for iteration and a locked test set.
debrief: Prompts can overfit just like models. The discipline of held-out test data applies.

subject: prompt-engineering
subtopic: Comparing prompts on a shared set
question: Is the AI right that this comparison is well designed and supports choosing B?

artifact.prompt:
Prompts A and B were each run on the same 200 held-out support tickets.
A rubric (correct category, required fields present, policy followed) was applied by two reviewers blind to which prompt produced each output.
Results: A 78%, B 86%; per-ticket comparison: B better on 31 tickets, A better on 15, tie on 154.

ai_claim: Yes. Both prompts saw identical tickets, reviewers were blind and used a rubric, and the paired comparison shows B winning on twice as many tickets as A, which supports B.

ai_solution.text: Identical held-out tickets make the comparison fair.
A rubric and blind reviewers reduce bias.
The paired results show B better on 31 tickets and A on 15.

canonical_solution: Correct. A paired comparison on the same held-out set with blind rubric grading is sound; 31 vs 15 is a clear advantage (a sign test gives p of about 0.03).

valid_evidence.summary: Per-ticket results: B better on 31, A better on 15.

hints.text: Check fairness, grading and statistics.
Step 3 uses a paired comparison.
Same inputs, blind rubric grading and paired analysis make comparisons trustworthy.
Look at the wins and losses per ticket.
This solution is correct. The comparison is sound and favours B. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: Paired comparisons on shared inputs are the most sensitive way to compare prompts.

subject: prompt-engineering
subtopic: A regression suite for prompt changes
question: Is the AI right that this process protects against prompt changes that break existing behaviour?

artifact.prompt:
Every prompt change triggers an automated suite: 150 saved cases (including 30 past failures and 20 injection attempts), with expected outputs or rubric checks.
The change ships only if no previously passing case fails.

ai_claim: Yes. Rerunning saved cases after each change catches regressions, including reintroducing fixed bugs and new injection weaknesses, before they reach users.

ai_solution.text: Past failures ensure fixed bugs stay fixed.
Injection attempts check that security holds.
Blocking releases on new failures prevents regressions shipping.

canonical_solution: Correct. Regression suites are as important for prompts as for code, because small wording changes can alter behaviour unexpectedly.

valid_evidence.summary: A wording change that shortened the prompt failed 4 of the 20 injection cases and was blocked.

hints.text: Ask what could go wrong when a prompt changes.
Step 2 keeps past fixes in place.
Regression tests protect existing behaviour during changes.
Consider a change that weakens injection resistance.
This solution is correct. The suite catches regressions. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: Treat prompts as code: version them, review them and test them on every change.

subject: prompt-engineering
question: Is prompt B better than prompt A?

artifact.prompt:
Prompt A: 81/100 correct. Prompt B: 84/100 correct.
The two prompts were run on different random samples of 100 tickets each; per-ticket results are not available.

ai_claim: Yes. B scored 84% against A's 81%, three points higher, so B is the better prompt.
missing_information: Whether the difference is larger than noise. With 100 different tickets per prompt, each accuracy has a standard error of about 4 percentage points, so a 3-point gap is well within chance; the samples may also differ in difficulty. A paired comparison on the same tickets is needed.
resolving_scenarios: On the same 300 tickets, B beats A on 25 and loses on 8: B is genuinely better.
On the same tickets, B wins 12 and loses 11: the prompts are equivalent, and the 3-point gap came from sample differences.
canonical_solution: The evidence cannot distinguish a real improvement from noise. Step 3 compares numbers from different samples without uncertainty.

valid_evidence.summary: Standard error of 82% with n = 100 is sqrt(0.82 x 0.18 / 100) = 0.038, about 4 points - larger than the gap.

counterexamples: Re-sampling 100 tickets could reverse the order.

hints.text: Estimate the uncertainty of each score.
Step 3 compares numbers from different samples.
Fair comparisons use the same inputs and account for noise.
Compute the standard error for 100 tickets.
Step 3 ignores noise and sample differences. B may or may not be better. It cannot be decided.

repair: Run both prompts on the same tickets and compare per-ticket results.
debrief: Small differences need paired evidence and uncertainty estimates.
